For a partial order \(P\) of width \(w\), some chain family \(\mathcal{C}\) of \(w\) chains has \({\preceq_{\mathcal{C}}} = {\preceq_{\mathcal{M}, P}}\).
Every chain family with fewer chains differs from \(P\) on some pair of decisions.
• all chains in \(\textcolor{dpred}{O(|\mathcal{M}|^2 \log |\mathcal{M}|)}\) time; then a genetic algorithm for chain families (Lai et al. 2020) optimizes over \(\textcolor{dpred}{\mathcal{C}}\)

Among the decisions that zero those first layers, \(x_0\) is Pareto optimal on the next layer.

• a layered extension of \(P\): each layer an antichain, each union \(B_1 \cup \cdots \cup B_l\) an upper set
  • its weights grow by one power of \(i\) per layer

• \(\mathcal{B}\) targets an upper set \(U\) if \(U = B_1 \cup \cdots \cup B_l\) and \(B_{l+1} = \operatorname{Max}(\mathcal{M} \setminus U)\)
  • if no decision zeroes more than \(\textcolor{dpred}{U}\), the limit zeroes \(\textcolor{dpred}{U}\) and is Pareto optimal on \(\textcolor{dpred}{\{m_1, m_4, m_7\}}\) under it
  • Not necessarily maximally zeroed as an upper set in \(P\): maybe one of \(m_1, m_4, m_7\) can further be zeroed, just not at the same time!
Targeting every upper set to get the maximally zeroed ones

The width of \(\sqsubseteq\) is the smallest number of layered extensions that together target every upper set but \(\mathcal{M}\).
This width is at most \((|\mathcal{M}| + 1)^w - 1\) and usually far less.
Here the width is 4, against the bound 15.

• \(U \sqsubseteq U'\): after \(U\), an extension goes on with \(\operatorname{Max}(\mathcal{M} \setminus U)\), and can still target \(U'\)
  • so one extension targets one chain of \(\sqsubseteq\), and the fewest extensions cover the upper sets by the fewest chains
  • here \(\emptyset, \{m_1\}, \{m_2\}, \{m_1, m_3\}\) are pairwise incomparable, so four extensions are needed, and they suffice
  • the green weights give \(\textcolor{dpgreen}{(\{m_1\}, \{m_3\}, \{m_2\})}\), which targets \(\textcolor{dpgreen}{\{m_1, m_3\}}\)

One need the family of every minimal layered extension.

Let every metric be \(\max\{f_m, 0\}\) with \(f_m\) strictly convex.
Then every family that targets every upper set gives \(\mathcal{X}^*_P\).

If \(d\) is posetally improving at \(x\), then \(x + t d \prec_{\mathcal{M},P} x\) for every small enough \(t > 0\).

• an oracle gives, for each metric \(m\) at \(x\), a cone \(C_{m,x}\) of directions that do not worsen \(m\), and whether it strictly improves \(m\)
  • \(d\) is posetally improving if some metric improves, and every metric whose cone misses \(d\) lies strictly below an improving one
  • every \(d\) comes with an upper set \(U\) that certifies the posetal improvement

Every certifying upper set holds each metric below no improvable metric, because such a metric can never be excused.

Take differentiable metrics and the gradient oracle.
Then \(x\) admits a posetally improving direction if and only if some \(d\) has \(\nabla m(x)^\top d < 0\) for every maximal metric \(m\).

• so a posetal descent is steepest descent on the maximal metrics (Fliege and Svaiter 2000), here \(m_1, m_2\)
  • convex is not enough: \(\textcolor{dpred}{m_1 = x_1^2}\) and \(\textcolor{dpred}{m_2 = x_2^2}\) at \(\textcolor{dpred}{(0, 1)}\) admit no improving direction, while \(\textcolor{dpred}{(0, 0)}\) is better
Strictly convex metrics: no improving direction means optimal

Let every metric \(m\) be \(\max\{f_m, c_m\}\) with \(f_m\) strictly convex.
Then \(x \in \mathcal{X}^*_P\) if and only if \(x\) admits no posetally improving direction.
• for differentiable strictly convex metrics, steepest descent on the maximal metrics is good enough: the less important metrics never matter
